conversation.content:
Hello—thank you for making time to talk with me today. I’m Dr. Bennett, a perinatal-mental-health clinician. My role is to check in on how mothers are feeling emotionally after childbirth, because the postpartum period can bring surprises that are hard to talk about.

We’ll be using a short questionnaire called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**, or EPDS for short. It’s simply a 10-item screen that helps us understand how your mood, energy, and thoughts have been over the past seven days. There are no right or wrong answers, and everything you share stays confidential within our care team. If any question feels uncomfortable, you can skip it or tell me you’d rather not answer.

I’ll read each item conversationally, and you can respond in your own words. When you’re ready, we’ll jump right in.

Here’s the first one:

Over the past week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

[Presses lips together, eyes downcast]

Honestly… I haven’t really laughed at all. I’ll see something on my phone that used to make me chuckle, and I just… can’t. It feels like there’s this weight on my chest that keeps even a smile from coming out. My husband tried to joke with me yesterday and I just nodded—nothing felt funny.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
I wish that were true for me… but no, I haven’t. Even when my baby makes those silly faces that used to crack me up, I just feel flat—like I’m watching through a fog.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really… I used to get excited about little stuff—coffee with a friend, a walk around the neighborhood—but now it all feels like another chore. I tell myself I *should* look forward to things, but mostly I’m just tired and kind of numb.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I do that a lot. If the baby’s fussy, I immediately think it’s because I’m not doing something right—maybe I ate the wrong thing, or I didn’t hold him long enough. Last night he wouldn’t settle and I just kept thinking, “I’m failing at this, I’m a terrible mom.” I know in my head it’s not all my fault, but the guilt keeps coming anyway.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much all the time. I’ll be feeding him and suddenly my heart’s racing because I’m sure he’s not breathing right, or I’ll lie down and think the ceiling fan is going to fall on him. Nothing’s actually wrong, but I can’t shake the fear that something awful’s about to happen.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yes… it hits me out of nowhere. I’ll just be sitting on the couch and suddenly my chest feels tight, like I can’t get enough air, and my mind jumps to worst-case scenarios—what if I drop him, what if he stops breathing in the night, what if I’m just not cut out for this. I know there’s no real danger, but the panic still sweeps over me.
Things have been getting on top of me

Mmm… most days, honestly. It’s like the laundry, the bottles, the night feedings, the texts I haven’t answered—they all pile up until I feel I’m drowning. Sometimes I sit on the nursery floor and just stare at the mess, frozen, wondering how everyone else seems to manage. I do get through it, but it feels like I’m barely keeping my head above water.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yeah… I’ll finally get the baby down, but then I lie there wide-awake, mind racing—replaying every little thing I did wrong, worrying about tomorrow, feeling this heavy sadness I can’t turn off. Some nights I just stare at the ceiling until the first morning cry comes.
I have felt sad or miserable

Most of the time, yeah. It’s like there’s this gray cloud hanging over everything. I’ll look at my baby and feel like I should be happier, but instead I just feel empty or weepy. Some mornings I wake up already sad, before anything’s even happened.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… it happens a few times a week. Sometimes it’s triggered—like when I can’t get him to nap or when I drop a bottle and formula goes everywhere—and other times it’s just this wave that hits out of nowhere. I’ll sit in the rocker with tears running down my face, feeling like I’m failing even when everything’s technically “fine.”
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No… I haven’t thought about hurting myself. I feel down and overwhelmed, but I’ve never wanted to end things—I just want to feel better and be a good mom.

You've shared that the past week has felt heavy-laughter and excitement seem distant, daily tasks feel like drowning, and waves of worry or panic arrive without warning. Even when your baby does something that once made you smile, a persistent gray cloud of sadness, guilt, and fatigue lingers. You cry often, blame yourself for every hiccup, and lie awake spinning worst-case scenarios, yet you clearly love your child and want to feel like "you" again.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 25, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient explicitly states inability to laugh despite previously enjoyable moments, matching "Not at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports almost total loss of anticipatory joy, describing activities as chores and feeling numb, aligning with "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Fallback score from text</sym>, <sym>Patient reports constant, intrusive, irrational worries occurring "pretty much all the time" with physical anxiety symptoms and catastrophic fears despite no real threat, matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden, intense panic episodes with physical symptoms and catastrophic thoughts occurring frequently.</sym>, <sym>The mother describes feeling overwhelmed "most days" and "barely keeping my head above water," aligning with "sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes persistent, severe insomnia driven by distress and sadness "most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports pervasive sadness "most of the time," persistent low mood, anhedonia, and morning despondency—clearly matching "Yes, most of the time."</sym>, <sym>Patient reports crying "a few times a week" from both situational and spontaneous triggers, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** EPDS scores of 25 far exceed the 14-point threshold for probable depression. She endorses core symptoms of major depressive disorder with peripartum onset: depressed mood most of the day, markedly diminished interest or pleasure (<sym>anhedonia</sm>), feelings of worthlessness (<sym>excessive guilt</sym>), fatigue, insomnia, and psychomotor slowing (<sym>freezing</sym>). Anxiety symptoms are prominent and co-occurring. No suicidal ideation (<sym>Q10=0</sym>). This pattern coupled with functional impairment places her in the high-risk category. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with <med>obstetric or primary care provider</med> for full psychiatric evaluation
2. Refer to <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med> for therapy (CBT or interpersonal therapy)
3. Discuss <med>antidepressant medication</med> options compatible with breastfeeding if indicated
4. Offer immediate <med>peer support group</med> or <med>postpartum doula</med> resources
5. Encourage 15-20 min daily outdoor walks and acceptance of help with night feeds to improve <sym>sleep</sym>
6. Provide 24-h crisis numbers and schedule follow-up EPDS in 1-2 weeks
7. Involve partner/family in safety and self-care plan
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 25: Screening Note – Postpartum Visit  
Date: [today’s date]  
Source: Self-report via EPDS-style questionnaire  

<sym>Symptoms endorsed</sym>  
- Persistent low mood, anhedonia (“gray cloud,” no pleasure in baby’s cues)  
- Daily tearfulness, feeling “empty” or “weepy” 3–4×/wk  
- Sleep disruption secondary to racing thoughts/guilt after infant settled  
- Excessive self-blame and guilt (“failing,” “terrible mom”)  
- Free-floating anxiety, panic spells (tight chest, “can’t get air”) focused on infant safety  
- Overwhelm/“drowning” with routine tasks, frequent freezing/staring  
- No suicidal ideation or self-harm intent (explicitly denied)

<med>Pattern</med>  
Symptoms cluster consistent with moderate–severe postpartum depression with prominent anxiety; functional impairment evident (household tasks “pile up,” social withdrawal).  
<med>Risk factors</med>: primiparous, self-criticism, sleep loss.  
<med>Protective factors</sm>: denies self-harm, expresses desire to “feel better and be a good mom.”

<med>Screening significance</med>  
Score suggests elevated probability of major depressive episode with comorbid anxiety; referral for comprehensive evaluation and follow-up monitoring recommended.
